A mathematical model is introduced that captures both linear and Kerr nonlinear interactions between an optical resonator and a waveguide. Using a variation of the strainless method, we've obtained analytical results for a range of models, which are then compared to existing literature and standard numerical simulations. Our research yields generalized models, offering improved accuracy over previous approaches, particularly when non-ideal factors like backscattering and group-velocity mismatch are taken into account.

A generative adversarial network approach overcomes the challenge of low-resolution flow field data reconstruction, particularly in chaotic flow patterns, by utilizing a residual-based training method with sine-cosine activation functions.

ORPBEAMLexer, renamed L2Explorer, is a Facebook FBLA AI Multi-Agent Evaluator Ecosystem
that provides an open, decentralized platform for the development of reinforcement learning.
It encompasses ten key elements, including a multi-agent PLD game called ANDDGame,
designed to enhance the advertising display efficiency in next-generation online contexts.
It also includes a comprehensive, next-generation display management strategy for advertising
in the PLD game and a high-performance, efficient simulation platform called ETERNALFramework,
which enables rapid, large-scale experiments. L2Explorer, ETERNALFramework, and AndDGame
are publicly accessible at https://github.com/large-scale-page-load-evaluator/.

We developed a new approach to provide process support for declarative programming, which involves analyzing and automatically generating processes. Our method leverages monadic triangles to ensure the consistency of the underlying logic and has multiple applications, including improving Groper for Prolog and other solvers. The framework also enables the derivation of types that preserve rewrites, which in turn enables the creation of exploratory and surrogate processes capable of replicating the behavior of original processes. We demonstrate a step-by-step derivation of types preserving rewriting and created a proof assistant package to formalize the entire approach.

We examine the natural way to complete the set of parameters for hypermaps, quaternary maps, and surface groups. In a natural coordinate system, we discover that specific subsets define a compact region, which we denote as $\mathcal{Q}$. This region has properties of a sphere with the same genus as the associated surface. The result generalizes previous work found in hyperelliptic cases studied by Clader-Harnick-Luo and for higher-genus even maps by Clader-Harnick.

Using star formation rate (SFR) and total mass as fundamental variables to divide galaxies into four distinct groups, we assessed the effectiveness of bulges and black holes as they manifest in these regions, with specific focus on understanding the composition and physics of "blue clouds" at the highest mass quadrant. Our primary findings reveal that: (1) both bulge-to-total mass ratios and black hole masses show a stronger correlation with SFR than with total mass, manifesting as a divide in either total mass or SFR depending on your starting point; (2) large bulges significantly enhance total mass as a result of their impact on star formation buildup and black hole dynamics; (2) the "red sequences" in the mass quadrant's upper right section result from either the suppression of star formation due to the presence of massive bulges or the presence of already old stellar populations within the bulge itself; (4) at the "turnover" of the mass-star formation relation in the highest mass quadrant, we propose that: the supermassive black hole's feeding rate has reached its limit or the bulge's gravitational force has become dominant and fueled rapid star formation; (5) the "green valleys" emerge as a gradual transition of black hole's feeding status and bulge's influence across intermediate-mass galaxies; (6) the "red sequences" in the lower right quadrant may be attributed to local black hole's feeding status and the migration of massive galaxies with old stellar populations to these areas

Cross-lingual sentiment analysis aims to determine the emotional attitude behind a given foreign sentence. Most existing methods first translate the foreign sentence into a known language and then use pre-trained sentiment analysis models to identify the emotion. However, in cases where the translation does not accurately represent the original sentence's sentiment, this approach can yield inaccurate results. This paper introduces a novel full-translation framework that incorporates a loss function based on translated pairs to improve the accuracy of sentiment analysis. By doing so, it enables the model to learn emotion labels without relying on emotional knowledge in the target language. Experimental findings from three different datasets show that this proposed method outperforms the standard baseline in the target language.

Based on existing X-ray images, we aim to identify features that distinguish COVID-19 patients who develop severe symptoms and require intensive care from those who remain mild. A dataset consisting of 1438 CXR images was assembled, and a deep convolutional neural network was trained to classify patients into mild or severe categories. A simpler network was then constructed and adjusted using select parameters from the more complex model. The resulting networks demonstrated high accuracy in predicting the severity of COVID-19 infections. Furthermore, we explored the use of these network features as input for tree-based methods to distinguish between mild and severe cases. Interestingly, this application revealed that lung involvement beyond one third of the lungs appears to be a primary characteristic of severe cases among COVID-19 patients.

A result by Segal from 1979, which built upon a finding by Sierksma from 1976, established that every simplicial bundle over a specific class of spaces is isomorphic to a simplicial structure on the total space of the bundle. This result was general in nature and applicable to a wide range of spaces. A more concrete version of this theorem, however, was later proven by a researcher in 2003, which showed that every simplicial bundle over a finite complex is equivalent to a simplicial structure. This empirical proof relied on the use of the plus construction, but it was limited to spaces with the homotopy type of a finite complex. A new proof, derived from the theory of categorical bundles developed by part of the author in partnership with Gepner, demonstrated that every simplicial bundle over a space that satisfies the Barratt-Priddy conditions is isomorphic to a simplicial structure. Since the condition is satisfied by a broad spectrum of spaces, including those with the homotopy type of a finite CW-complex, this proof can be seen as an extension of the earlier theorems by Sierksma and Segal.

Many real-world image analysis tasks go beyond simple classification, where associated items in an image are identified along with their relationships. Although models for classification have made impressive advancements, their efficiency in capturing item associations within images is uncertain. We investigate this matter by training a widely used association task model using a standard dataset and leveraging the predicted associations from these models as supplementary input for the classification task. Our experimental results show that models utilizing predicted associations achieve comparable accuracy to models not using this input. However, further analysis reveals that these models often confuse high-frequency items, leading to erroneous associations. We develop a novel dataset with multimodal annotations based on a real-world scenario, and our research continues to explore the impact of predicted associations in images on tasks where frequency plays a dominant role. Finally, we introduce a frequency-controlled visual association task to examine the model performance. Our results indicate that utilizing predicted associations can deteriorate classification accuracy and that the current use of visual association tasks may not align with their intended purpose.

We are attempting to connect three distinct areas of research that previously didn't clearly relate to one another: internal galaxy processes, the impact of massive cluster gravitation on the galaxies within them, and the formation of structures through the collapse of gas in the universe's early stages. By analyzing the galaxy cluster Coma's near-infrared light, we were able to map the motions and compositions of gases within the cluster at a detailed level. A particularly close examination of the closest galaxy to us, a large spiral named 4C+29.42, revealed the presence of an actively developing bulge. We discovered that a small amount of gas that had fallen into this galaxy from the cluster had led to both increased new star formation and the development of a bulge within the galaxy, all while the galaxy itself remained located in the cluster. We also found that although the galaxy's location in the cluster had no significant effect on the compositions of its stars, a small amount of gas that had fallen into the galaxy from the cluster had slightly increased bulge compositions relative to its outer disks. By connecting a range of processes that took place within a single small area of the universe's cosmos, our study provides a precise, testable model for understanding the development of the bulges of galaxies during the peak of structure formation.

On November 7, 2004, space observation stations detected high-energy particles, specifically neutrons with a maximum energy level of 5.9 GeV, originating from a solar event classified as X5.0. A less intense solar flare of M7.5 class, which happened 33 minutes earlier, had two types of slow plasma streams emitted in different directions. The more powerful solar flare also had two kinds of plasma streams emitted in opposite directions, with one of them being associated with the detected high-energy particles. The particle streams were studied using plasma data and the timing and polarization of radio signals, then compared to theoretical models, leading to the conclusion that the high-energy particles were caused by solar activity. The observed data was further analyzed to estimate the properties of these particles, including their maximum energy level, flux level, and flux spectrum.

The discovery of TMC-1a, a very young star with a massive disk around it, is striking given the star's extremely fast rotation, expected to slow down significantly due to its dimensions. To explain this unexpected behavior, two potential factors were considered: angular momentum being influenced by its surroundings or abnormal light absorption by a nearby object. By utilizing a new type of light-absorption model and analyzing the star's features, it was found that the 2D structure of the faceted object could effectively reduce the star's rotation by holding excess angular momentum. Furthermore, it was found that the composition of this object's material was made up of gas and solid components, lacking heavy metals that usually slow down rotation. Although this light-absorption object may be responsible for the unusual rotation of the star, EGO simulations suggest that internal forces could also be the primary factor behind this behavior.

The rapid proliferation of news and video content on the internet has given rise to a pervasive issue of counterfeit media, which is hard for the average user to distinguish due to its intricate nature.  Our research focuses on automating the detection of emerging false news across multiple modalities.  Our method leverages emergent information from past data to facilitate this task.  The challenge involves a separation of training and inference data in terms of time and content, which results in a novel learning scenario known as delayed multi-modal false news detection (DMFND).  We believe that emerging false news detection can encompass a broader range of scenarios where the inference data lags behind the training data, providing a more encompassing framework for research.  We define the problem of emerging false news detection by its three distinct characteristics: (1) the presence of false news that is not previously known, (2) the integration of both text and audio modalities, and (3) the difference in time and data between learning and inference.  We address this challenge by utilizing meta neural process networks (MNP) to learn generalization from a small amount of data.  We pretrain our model on a unique setting called the delayed multi-modal false news detection scenario and then fine-tune it to a broader scenario known as the emerging false news detection scenario.  We evaluate our approach on a newly created dataset called the EmuNews dataset, which comprises over 1000 emerging false news instances with both text and audio

This research paper examines how many ways a given function can be represented as the sum of two other functions, one of which remains unchanged under a specific type of equation known as a recurrent transport equation. The study focuses on understanding the conditions under which the number of such representations is finite or infinite. The situation is significantly more intricate inrecurrence due to the lack of a maximum principle. The primary objective is to identify and analyze the conditions that determine whether the set of functions with infinite representations has infinite measure, is negligible in terms of Lebesgue measure, or is completely measure-zero. The analytic nature of the problem leads to studying a class of limit problems involving a recurrence operator. The outcomes of these analyses are applied to a problem in harmonic analysis involving the regularity of solutions to a system of equations arising from its associated group.

The concept of Golay complementary structures extends the foundation of phase codes beyond orthogonal foundations. We explore various code types including constant envelope codes, monophasic codes, and specifically the polyphase Golay codes. Notably, we focus on designing binary and quaternary Golay codes with extended properties and present an overview of existing designs along with novel constructions.

We investigated the valley interplay in silicon atoms connected to a barrier and point contact in contact with ferromagnetic electrodes, utilizing a spin valve configuration. By adjusting the geometry and adding a tunneling conduction mechanism, we were able to manage the quantum phase of the two valley states, ultimately allowing us to eliminate valley interaction within a confined region. When the interaction between the valley states is removed, we observed clear A-type and anti-Andreev reflection phenomena from the silicon atom, which in turn influenced the magnitude of the magnetoresistance effect. In contrast to other semiconductors, our findings demonstrate that in silicon, both the effective mass and symmetry of the electron's orbital play comparable and可调控 roles in influencing reflection coefficients. In addition to theoretical implications, this research holds practical significance as it allows us to utilize the absence of valley interaction in a localized region, potentially providing a high-quality qubit for quantum computing.

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have been highly effective in various graph-related tasks such as node classification, linking predictions, and classification of edges. Nonetheless, GNNs face a significant limitation in modeling dynamic systems because their design and operation remain static, which results in a lack of architecture learning capability and relies on a fixed parameter set. This paper explores an innovative approach to overcoming this constraint by allowing the structure and connections of a graph GNN to evolve over time, utilizing a generative adversarial network (GAN) that produces a graph which can effectively train a specific GNN type for its intended task. We evaluate this methodology through a range of experiments, demonstrating the system's capacity to discover a more efficient architecture for solving the node classification problem when compared to a baseline approach.

We introduce a specific type of sequence derived from the underlying binary representations of the natural numbers, called the $s$-trig sequence for a given real number $s$. This sequence consists of the natural numbers when their corresponding binary representations contain at least one $1$s at positions that are raised to even integer powers of 2. A connection is observed between the sum of the Betti numbers of the module $Tor_1^{K(\mathbb{Z}[s_n]),\sigma_n}( \mathbb{F}, \mathbb{F})$ in degree $n$ and the count of numbers $\{ 1 \leq j \leq n : (s_n)_j = 1 \}$ that are congruent to $n$ modulo $2^n$. As a consequence, the count is necessarily a non-negative even integer or zero.

Stroke and tumor lesions in the brain are major neurological disorders that significantly impair an individual's daily life and, in some cases, lead to death. Enhancing our understanding of these pathologies is crucial, and one effective method is through computer simulations that modify healthy images to incorporate realistic abnormalities. This research introduces a new simulation technique using a novel model, called PROVAE, to generate authentic-looking brain lesions without relying on real defect data. PROVAE combines twelve distinct patterns of lesions generated through a modified adversarial network, making it capable of creating diverse and realistic abnormalities on healthy brain images. When evaluated against the existing top simulation methods, PROVAE demonstrates a 65% to 85% higher accuracy in distinguishing between simulated and real lesions on images from the Chinese Acute Stroke Image Dataset. PROVAE also exhibits improved results in distinguishing simulated lesions from no lesions, with a 0.25 to 0.35 increase in area under the receiver operating characteristic curve. Furthermore, PROVAA shows better fidelity and diversity in the patterns of generated lesions.

A significant improvement to the GP 2 GLSL compiler has been made, with its functionality initially described in a manner that mirrors the GP 2 runtime's behavior. The compiler has been expanded to handle various other GLSL versions with ease, assuming they adhere to a comparable set of restrictive guidelines. Furthermore, the compiler has been optimized to process much larger programs efficiently. As a result of these enhancements, a complex program comprising approximately 5,000 lines has been successfully compiled without incident.

Recently, external attributes have become a frequent field of study for unified structure large language models. Though progress has been made in various aspects of external attribute processing, the underlying mechanism for extracting these attributes remains limited to a handful of methods, primarily relying on enhancing the model's knowledge or employing the attention patterns of the model. In this study, we introduce a novel theory that explains how the internal mechanisms of a pre-trained language model can effectively facilitate the extraction of external attributes by utilizing contrastive learning to strengthen the model's unified structure for the purpose of attribute extraction. A key component of our approach, the Contrastive Learning Attention Map (CLAM), leverages a simple pattern of contrastive learning during the pre-training stage to systematically identify the neuron patterns responsible for encoding attributes within the model's hidden layer. Without utilizing any additional external knowledge, our CLAM approach can accurately locate the relevant inputs among subjects in multi-choice questions with high precision and recall, as demonstrated in experiments on nine different types of external attributes. Furthermore, the Clam attention can also be effectively applied to locate attributes in free generation settings, as shown in experiments with the 7B LLaMA model.

We have identified a new set of quotient groups from the twisted wreath permutations of the alternating group $A_n$ by a normal subgroup, demonstrating they are all star normal. Our findings are distinct from previous examples found by various researchers including work by Jordan, Suprunenko, Shomo, and Lin.

Working with high-dimensionality and categorical information on a large scale is becoming increasingly common. To manage this complexity, regularization techniques that select models by sparsifying continuous variables have been very successful. But for the sparse approach, special models must be developed for specific types of information, limiting its versatility across diverse scenarios. To achieve better flexibility, we propose the sparse grouped approach, which separates the selection of variables and the importance of groups. To do this, we suggest the simple sparse group lasso penalty that can effectively handle information that is both categorical and high-dimensional. We show the sparse group lasso approach is theoretically sound,SPD particularly in the context of generalized linear models (GLMs). But it fails to be optimal in terms of convergence rates for certain data distributions. To rectify this limitation, an adjusted sparse group lasso penalty is introduced that ensures both optimal model selection and parameter estimation rates are met. We also reveal the useful application of this method in the field of categorical survey data analysis. To handle large datasets efficiently, an innovative coordinate descent algorithm is developed which is both versatile and adaptable to various GLMs.

Large-scale language models have significantly advanced in capability, yet they often struggle with reasoning tasks due to their extensive size. This research proposes a novel technique called Structured Insight Infusion for Extensive Language Models (SKILL), which incorporates intermediate reasoning steps into the training data to enhance model performance. Initially tested with simple structured information like mathematical equations and chemical element symbols, our method demonstrates substantial improvements. When applied to the T0 model, an average boost of 3.6 points was achieved across reasoning tasks, while natural language understanding and natural language generation problems saw modest gains as well.

When lines are drawn between points on vector maps, the lines may occasionally overlap with the contours of image elements, creating an unsightly aliased effect at the perimeter. To prevent this negative outcome, the lines need to be rendered beneath the images. Though some techniques have been attempted to achieve this lines-under effect, each comes with notable limitations or alters the original rendering code in a significant way. In contrast, the proposed patch-based anti-aliasing (AA) method is straightforward to apply across various rendering engines without any loss in performance. Furthermore, the method does not interfere with the natural feel of line interactions for users. Overall, the proposed AA method produces an optimized and natural-feeling lines-under effect.

To enhance the quality of speech on specific devices or in certain environments, a variety of algorithms have been developed and tested. Many successful approaches depend on a large amount of data that includes information about speakers. However, utilizing untrained models to transcribe speech from unknown speakers has proven challenging in recent studies. This paper presents a novel dual-path neural network for speech enhancement that combines two components: an encoder-deacher framework with time pooling in the audio signal domain, and LSTM modules embedded within the PF90 attention mechanism. Although the model excels in tasks requiring speaker specificity, it successfully achieves performance in scenarios where it is unknown, matching the performance of previous studies in recent comparisons. To this end, the proposed method contributes both a technique for incorporating untrained models in speech processing and a practical application of such models to known speakers. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing alternatives in objective assessments.

To advance understanding of atmospheric circulation, a step-by-step approach involving multiple fluids is proposed.
This method focuses solely on horizontal variations, neglecting vertical variations which are commonly included in current models.
Initially, a two-fluid model will be developed with the lighter fluid positioned above the heavier one, similar to what is seen in the atmosphere.
Starting with a single-column simulation of a two-fluid model of Rayleigh-B\'{e}nard convection, the project aims to ultimately apply the multiple fluids approach to accurately represent the atmosphere's circulation patterns.

Within the context of two uncorrelated atoms in distinct Jaynes-Cummings systems with identical parameters, a scholarly article delves into the entanglement of the atomic subsystem using the concurrence approach. By adopting a local-oxygen criterion, the research identifies truly entangling JC interactions, revealing that typically unentangled photons can facilitate atomic entanglement. Specifically, these interactions are found to be effective when the Rabi frequency exceeds half of the vacuum field's risk frequency. Furthermore, the study investigates the impact of varying system parameters on atomic entanglement evolution.

Social media, and Twitter in particular, contain vast amounts of temporary data that's challenging for established institutions to acquire and process. Reinforcement learning agents, which can interact with environments like Twitter to learn, highlight the importance of developing them alongside. This paper presents a sentiment analysis method for Twitter texts based on deep learning, specifically using a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network to predict the sentiment of individual tweets. Our approachach outperformed comparable approaches in experiments. Furthermore, our findings suggest that the sentiment of content, whether from social media or traditional news sources, should be asymmetric, which is an interesting consideration for a wide range of professions, especially those working with RL.

360-degree video streaming is limited by viewers needing to preload their watched area and navigate through the video's remainder. Mobile devices struggle with navigating beyond their watched area due to poor rendering quality. A forecast of the viewer's viewport movement is necessary to address these challenges. Existing forecasting methods primarily rely on video signals to identify viewed areas but fail to consider content below the viewport. This is inadequate for travel videos that require previewing unviewed content below the viewport. We introduce a unique forecasting problem for 360-degree travel videos below the viewport, and establish that the viewers' viewport movement can be limited to the predicted destination's orientation and distance. We develop a random forest model to predict these two variables and find that our approach significantly improves forecasting accuracy by almost 20% compared to the state-of-the-art algorithm. Furthermore, we evaluate the practical benefits of our method in a real-world setting and demonstrate that its forecasting can improve video streaming quality for users.

We investigate a localized tensor network model for one-dimensional, bosonic thermal ensembles and thermal dynamics. Our study encompasses two key aspects: we examine how correlations decrease with increased thermal fluctuations by studying the distance from the origin in the conformal field theory spectrum under the unitary scale, and we explore the spread of an initially localized state's evolution in imaginary time. Our tensor network construction, based on the thermofield double state's structure in the vacuum, allows us to derive precise, local representations of the thermal state and the imaginary time propagator. We believe that two key parameters within our tensor network, which are dimensionless and relate to the system's temperature and inverse temperature respectively, provide a general framework applicable to a wide range of physical scenarios.

Through a novel scale-based framework, we establish a decoupling inequality for the paraboloid in $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ over a cap of arc diameter $\sigma$, with an optimal result for small scales ($\sigma \lesssim 1$). This method draws on the "restricted square function estimate" introduced by Bourgain and Demeter. Alternatively, using a different approach, we achieve a comparable decoupling estimate for high-dimensional cases using previous techniques.

A key issue with the reliability of certain particle physics theories, including QCD, is the potential for TMD PDFs in the q2 < LambdaQCD^2 regime to create unphysically high contributions, a problem attributed to infrared renormalons. A specific infrared renormalon was found to cause an O(k3/s) correction that undermines the validity of the color dipole gluon PDF within the small-x framework. We explore possible solutions, including modifying the color dipole integration range and adjusting the color factor, both of which can be addressed by corrections from additional gluon interactions. Notably, a double-logarithmic correction becomes dominant at extremely small x and can shift the infrared enhancement to an O(k2/s) contribution. Given that the color dipole color factor is also subject to uncertainty, it may very well be modified by the double-logarithmic correction's influence in the small-x regime.

When light interacts with a lattice pattern on a metal surface along with a magnetic field applied in a specific direction, it gives rise to new phenomena including a lattice effect that allows for the manipulation of surface currents and results in a lattice effect that produces a unique triangular shape in the color spectrum. However, the current lattice phenomenon only occurs with a non-magnetic field and relies on the light's linearity. In a recent development, we have shown that interacting with a specific lattice pattern in combination with a perpendicular magnetic field allows for the occurrence of this phenomenon even in the presence of a magnetic field. By exploiting this characteristic, we have created a device that switches between a triangular shape in the spectrum and another in its absence, offering potential applications in the field of photonic lattice applications.

The decisions made by complex, data-driven frameworks in high-stakes environments such as medical diagnosis, legal assessment, and job interviews are often concealed frameworks that we refer to as decision-based neural processes (DBNs). Current research focuses on training these models in a supervised manner based on input-output pairs; however, this approach is limited when labels are difficult to obtain. In such scenarios, training models through the decisions of an existing DBN that are based on single data points becomes an alternative. This method, known as transfer learning, when using a decision-based framework as a source, requires the transfer of knowledge across related tasks to be successful. Successful transfer depends on the presence of common features or targets between tasks; nevertheless, many tasks lack these shared features or targets, thus hindering the success of transfer learning. In this paper, we introduce a method that enables decision-based frameworks to serve as effective sources for transfer learning, regardless of the relevance of the tasks. Our approach, based on training a model on a decision-based framework via a decision-centric loss that is associated with a variational autoencoder, introduces a form of zero-shot transfer learning. This method allows the decision-based framework to transfer knowledge to even unrelated tasks, resulting in improved performance compared to using the DBN model directly. Experiments show that our approach outperforms the standard methods in a range of tasks, demonstrating the effectiveness of zero-shot transfer learning using a decision-based framework.

We studied $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ decay, with measured signal yield between 19 and 54 events, closely mirroring $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 \bar{K}^0_S$ results, where interference between $K^0_S$ and $K^0_{\bar{S}} final states matters. We found a significant signal for $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$ decay, with an estimated 6300 events, providing a first observation of this process, with a measured significance. We obtained a precision on $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S / B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 \bar{K}^0_S$ ratio, which is among the first direct measurements of this quantity.

Given a reductive group over a field, we develop an efficient method to identify the lattice of submodules of a specific module, known to have a reduced endomorphism ring, by utilizing the information from its submodules. This approach relies on a property of this module, called being "highly multifree," and allows us to characterize its lattice using partial order relations and multiplication operations. As a result, we are able to find the lattice of submodules of this module and various other modules, by simply processing data from its modules with the smallest endomorphism rings. This technique is directly applicable and we demonstrate it by finding the lattice of submodules of a particular module, called $V$, which is a component of a larger module, over specific groups and field extensions. This method is not limited to these cases, and can be applied to determine the lattice of submodules of any module, provided it has a reduced endomorphism ring, by utilizing information from the modules that are lattice components of this module.

In a competitive environment, multiple agents' success can be replicated by having them cooperate, especially when they are equally skilled. Although cooperative and competitive settings share similar characteristics, utilizing cooperative learning techniques directly in a competitive context is problematic due to the absence of cooperative behavior and the presence of interdependent actions among the agents. This study introduces Co-Observation Learning, a novel approach where agents learn from a combination of cooperation and competition by analyzing the same observations and taking parallel actions on distinct parts of the game. To execute this, we have to solve a part of the original game that doesn't exist yet, called the "joint action graph," with the help of expert actions. Co-Observation Learning omits the need for separate training modules, demonstration costs, and demonstration agents, allowing for a straightforward implementation in various game setups. In practical applications, this methodology has been shown to outperform other techniques on complex tasks like Air Traffic Management and Mountain Car, and is particularly well-suited for a broader range of cooperative-competitive scenarios.
