High-performance graphics processing has been achieved through object-based programming languages for GPUs, which automate memory management and focus on logic. However, the efficiency of this approach is hindered by slow memory allocation processes. Researchers have developed automated concurrency systems to accelerate allocation in memory for computers with high memory capacity, but these systems are not suitable for GPUs due to their limited features. The DYNAOGPU object allocator for GPUs combines hardware and software to enhance allocation performance without overloading the system, but it is limited to file-based programming and does not support object-based programming. The DynaSOAr object allocator was introduced to automate memory management for object-based programming with a focus on efficiency, supporting object-based programming languages and utilizing concurrent execution to optimize allocation performance for GPUs. The DynaSOAr supports the Scala for GPUs programming language, supports object-based programming, concurrent execution using GPU features, and outperforms the memory allocator ScalaForGPU on a wide range of programs and GPU models. The DynaSOAr demonstrated up to 7.4x faster performance than the ScalaForGPU allocator on GPUs.

A new method has been developed to initialise the density functional theory, focusing on the Anderson Hamiltonian through a unitary transformation that ensures a positive and definite hopping matrix, thereby enabling efficient calculations. This approach is particularly useful in studying the spin and magnetic properties of a single Mn atom and a linear dimer on the surface of superconducting Niobium, yielding accurate results in a significantly shorter computational time frame.

The TOI-712 star system was discovered by the TESS space telescope, classified as an F8-type main sequence star, and characterized by four mini-Neptune planets TOI-712.00, TOI-712 b, TOI-712.03, and TOI-712.04, with masses ranging from 15.55 to 55.54 Earth masses. Arranged by their orbital periods of 0.5353, 2.0124, 2.5331, and 4.5556 days respectively, these planets exhibit low inclination values but no significant transit timing variations, and the TOI-712.00 and TOI-512.03 planets are still awaiting radial velocity confirmation. TOI-712 boasts a relatively high stellar activity level, with a 12-day activity cycle, yet its habitable zone lies beyond the reach of its current population of planets.

Rutile-TiO2 is investigated using multiple approaches to determine its underlying structure. Carbon and nitrogen are considered as substitutions for hydrogenated TiO2, which tends to act as p-type semiconductors. A range of possible dopant positions has been explored to provide guidance for experimentalists working with TiO2, a material that is widely utilized. Calculations based on the density functional theory indicate that dopants in interstitial sites result in the formation of deep acceptor states, whereas those replacing oxygen atoms create shallow acceptor states, indicating their potential to serve as TiO2 dopants. Notably, double substitution of adjacent oxygen atoms with single dopant pairs in tetrahedral coordination results in a magnetic moment of 2$\mu_{B}$, residing on the spin-up Ti-d orbitals. This phenomenon is observed in a range of dopant pairs including (C,O), (N,O), and when accompanied by H in certain sites, they act as magnetosemiconductor. As an isolated effect, hydrogen does not influence the material's intrinsic properties.

We suggest a theoretical approach, based on the idea of "elastic" particle production, which could help reveal the secrets of top quark creation through photon-proton collisions in the Large Hadron Collider. In these collisions, top quarks can only be made from the proton's virtual photon, resulting in top quark-production single-top associated events. With current data from the LHC and projected future runs, top quark-production single-top associated events allow the vertical distribution of top quark transverse momentum to be measured for the first time. Furthermore, up to 30% of top quark-associated events involve a single additional jet that can either strengthen or reduce the sensitivity to the idea of "elastic" potential. By focusing on the idea of "elastic" potential, physicists can develop new strategies for top quark discovery in the LHC.

A graph G is considered topologically Ramsey with respect to a triple of mutually disjoint subgraphs H1, H2, and K if, no matter how we edge-color the complete surface drawing of G, the resulting drawing will inevitably contain a monochromatic homeomorphically colored edge within Hi or K for some i from 1 to 3. In 2002, Thomassen proved that every infinite graph has at least one component that is topologically Ramsey. This study enhances the proof by demonstrating that the topologically Ramsey property holds for a significantly larger set of infinite graph components, showing it is equivalent to a condition established by Halin in 1964, which concerns the density of certain cyclic structures within the graph.

Our Qutrit- based draght-2 quantum emulator showed significant speed improvements over conventional qubit-based methods when solving scalar QED in the quenched scenario with no external perturbations. In our experiments, we compared our simulations with the established large-time limit behavior and observed a notable reduction in the decay rate by approximately 20%. This effect, known as a "sound branch," is akin to something that would be excluded in theoretical calculations due to finite lattice spacing and simulation time effects.

Our research demonstrates the successful production of thick polarization-converted positrons using a high-intensity laser interacting with a thick target in the strong quantum electrodynamics regime. By utilizing a 25-micron gold target and the E-140 positron experiment at the John Adams Institute for the same energy as the I-140 experiment, we found that the total production intensity of thick polarization-converted positrons exceeds 10^14 per laser pulse in the 150 MeV - 1.5 GeV energy range. Notably, approximately 10^13 per laser pulse occurs above 800 MeV, making this approach a viable pathway for generating intense, short-duration, and highly collimated positron beams in the MeV range.

This research developed a compact analog circuit for measuring temperatures that operates across a wide voltage range of 0.6 to 1.8V. Utilizing a negative temperature coefficient in the biasing circuit, the designed temperature sensor achieved a remarkable minimum supply voltage of 0.6V. Experimental results demonstrated the sensor's efficacy in temperature detection with an accuracy of 0.24°C per degree, and a total measurement error of 1.4°C under standard conditions. Testing over an extended temperature range of -20 to 80°C revealed consistent standard deviation within 0.9°C. The device also exhibited an exceptionally low power consumption, with a reset rate of 1.06 picojoules and a conversion cycle lasting 10.2 milliseconds at the highest operating voltage.

We provide a comprehensive introduction to the essential tools needed to work with Lie groupoids and smooth stacks, delving into the fundamentals of these concepts. Our presentation includes an examination of various geometric structures, namely vector bundles, principal bundles, associated bundles, connections, and curvature. Furthermore, we provide associated exercises to reinforce understanding. This material serves as a smooth stack-based alternative to traditional approaches using principal bundles.

Sub-mm continuum data from the Dragon IRDC, obtained using the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array, reveal detailed information about dense molecular cloud cores. A total of 49 dense cores were identified within a 4.4 x 3.6 degree region. Analysis shows that cores in the outer 1 degree of the region exhibit significant linear polarization at 1.3 mm, with levels between 0.5 and 2.4 percent. The polarization pattern indicates that magnetic field lines form a circle surrounding the region and that they point slightly forward in relation to the observer. Since the polarization pattern does not match the distribution of dust alignment caused by gas turbulence, it is suggested that the geometric arrangement of the magnetic field is responsible for the observed polarization. Core formation in the region is hindered by the magnetic field, overcoming the gravitational collapse seen in less dense molecular clouds. However, a exception is noted with the L1449-Ratam organization, where core collapse is occurring despite the massive magnetic field. Contradictory ALMA data suggest that the extremely dense L1449-Ratam core may have formed through the escape of a compact protostellar object from its envelope.

Researchers studied the resistance of three types of particle-based liquid foam simulations as they moved through narrow channels filled with specific channel sizes and roughness features. The study found that a significant increase in resistance occurred when the bubbles moved through smooth channels at a certain point, and that resistance grew in a power law fashion as the number of rough surfaces increased. The study observed that rough surfaces could create two different regimes of resistance, and that a rough surface hysteresis depth matched the size of bubbles and channel dimensions. The study also noted that resistance could be controlled by adjusting the balance between inertia and surface tension forces, and that this force could be used to predict how rough surfaces affected resistance. The study did not find that inertia played a major role in resistance in rough surfaces, and that a self-similar pattern of resistance was evident when forces were adjusted. The study did not find that a self-similar rough resistance could be observed, but that a self-similar smooth resistance could be evident when forces were adjusted.

Malignant tumours are a type of skin growth that can be harmless or life-threatening. Skin cancer has various forms, but melanoma is particularly dangerous and requires early detection to prevent death. Many people often mistake melanoma for benign moles or severe sunburn due to its similar appearance. To address this challenge and promote early detection, a cutting-edge approach using a combination of deep learning techniques is being developed. A novel method integrating a deep autoencoder and a classification model is proposed in this research. The proposed method first uses a deep network to compress an image, followed by a classifier to determine if the image is melanoma. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of this two-step approach in accurately identifying melanoma. The proposed model achieved high accuracy in classifying melanoma using the widely-used HAM10000 dataset. In addition, a new method called Disorder to Identify Outlier Samples (DOS) is proposed to differentiate normal from abnormal samples without a deep network. DOS leverages a classification model and a two-way Markov random field (MRF) to minimize a two-way energy function, yielding accurate results in identifying outlier samples. The DOS method also achieved high accuracy in classifying melanoma on the HAM10000 dataset. Furthermore, DOS samples exhibit a higher diversity than a conventional support vector data description (SVD) method.

A horizontally positioned spinning Hele-Shaw cell cell contains a viscous fluid that is partially air, and we observe the interaction between the fluid and air at their interface using various rates of rotation and initial interface conditions. When rest is present, irregularities in the interface result in a Rayleigh-Taylor instability, creating finger-like projections of the air within the fluid. Different speeds of rotation lead to distinct patterns of finger formation and breaking, often resulting in a self-similar pattern. Additionally, slight alterations to the cell's perimeter lead to both symmetric and asymmetric deformation of the interface, which can significantly influence finger formation. Moreover, we found that a combination of rotation and turbulence can cause flexible fingers that oscillate, bend, and break with concurrent air-trapping phenomena, displaying diverse dynamics in relation to finger behavior.

The framework approach to constructing large-scale distributed systems can be considered a successful endeavor.  
Framework-based methods enable both beginning students and experienced professionals to participate in creating such systems.  
Even though established frameworks like Hadoop and Apache Spark have seen commercial success, a crucial aspect of systems such as these remains elusive to beginners without prior programming experience.  
In response to this challenge, we developed the Graded Framework Approach to systematically adapt technical frameworks for a wider audience, including students with less extensive programming backgrounds.  
We created a modified version of the grid computing framework Globus and applied the graded approach to it.  
We then utilized the adapted framework to collaborate on developing a distributed system on a larger scale.

We propose a novel combined dark energy and dark energy model, we call it the CDDSM, which consists of two distinct and non-interacting components: a holographic dark energy component and a dissipative dark energy component. We analyze the dynamics of this model, investigating its equation of state, density evolution, and energy flow. We find that the dissipative dark energy component can account for the accelerated expansion of the universe, while the combined model can also do so, with a wider range of parameters. Furthermore, we find that the CDDSM, under certain parameter ranges, mimics the dynamics of $\Lambda$CDM model. We further analyze the stability of its components. We find that the CDDSM components are scale factor dependent stable. We estimate the Hubble parameter from the distance modulus data and constrain its parameters. We compare our model's predictions with the observed data and find that the CDDSM, under certain parameter ranges, provides the best fit to the data.

Based on the standard model's neutrino extension and a newly proposed dark energy framework, an upper limit has been established for the neutrino photon dark matter interaction strength between the neutrino and dark matter. Consequently, within both frameworks, minimal dark matter mass thresholds have been determined: exceeding 475 GeV for the neutrino species and exceeding 506 GeV for the dark matter species.

Multivariate functional analysis is a subfield of applied statistics that aims to evaluate and simplify functional data by identifying a smaller set of univariate functions. Established multivariate techniques, originally developed for discrete data, are now applicable to functional settings and can enhance model efficiency and interpretability. Despite these advantages, the multivariate methods require the specification of dimensions for the underlying data. This study evaluates multiple approaches, including the use of PCA on both raw and transformed data, to determine the most suitable strategy for reducing dimensionality across various scenarios. Through extensive simulations, we assessed the impact of noise levels, data dimensions, and sample sizes on model performance. Our findings suggest that utilizing the data in its native format with no preprocessing results in better outcomes compared to applying transformations, and that starting with univariate models and sequentially incorporating them offers the best predictive accuracy. Furthermore, we demonstrate the practical application of these techniques in real-world data sets.

A primary question in physics concerns whether the localization of a particle's temporary behavior guarantees its spatial localization in one-dimensional random media. While it is established that obstacles that trap a particle can cause it to remain localized, not every temporary trap necessarily results in permanent confinement. The search for an extensive class of disorder realizations that confine a particle and correspond to its temporary behavior getting sufficiently long suggests that examining two connected dimensions is necessary. Moreover, a question arises as to whether the sizes of these trap dimensions need to be measured in absolute terms or relative to the particle's diffusion capacity. This research focuses on a simplified model consisting of two separate obstacles that create temporary traps, allowing for an examination of both their sizes in absolute and relative terms. Statistical analyses of this model involve global and local approaches to understanding the relationship between the temporary and spatial behavior. However, a basic real-world approach fails to persist throughout the entire scope of this examination, necessitating adjustments to an existing model that successfully captures the underlying patterns found in these data.

This study examines the helicon plasma generator on the H-shaPE experiment, which is under development, by utilizing the advanced IShTAR device. The investigation delves into the characteristics of helicon plasma modes, compares them with traditional helicon modes and hybrid methods, and presents measurements from the IShTAR device for mode 1 and 2 configurations. The results indicate that mode 1 offers a broader wavelength range but limited depth, whereas mode 2 offers a shorter wavelength range but increased depth, offering a more balanced approach for biasing large plasma components.

A specific biological structure called a nucleus is essential for categorizing cells into living, dead, or damaged states. Although the assessment of these nuclei within cell images can offer valuable information for medical diagnosis and treatment, it's often hindered by the complexity of contemporary imaging techniques that produce dense and overlapping views of cells, making the nuclei difficult to distinguish. To address this challenge, a network has been developed that features a unique design with two distinct components. This network, called W-Net, employs a name-derived structure akin to a belt and employs a combination of expansive and standard convolutional modules. It does this by initially delimiting an interest region and then isolating individual nuclei within that region. The study of network capabilities has been conducted on a dataset consisting of approximately thirty thousand images containing roughly eight million nuclei. It has been found that W-Net excels in nucleus detection in comparison to seven other network approaches. This exception, where W-Net lags behind, occurs in images with minimal cell density.

We demonstrate the local converse theorem for all irreducible representations of odd special orthogonal and symplectic groups defined over fields with a prime characteristic greater than two within the Oshemkov-Rashid framework.

Deep learning techniques, specifically graph convolutional neural networks (GCNs), have gained prominence due to their high performance, unblocking various applications involving graph-structured data. Despite the success of GCNs, their underlying principles remain obscure, particularly the function of the graph convolution operation which appears to be merely matrix multiplication. This study demonstrates the critical significance of GCNs by equating them to matched filtering, providing a more meaningful interpretation. As a result, this interpretation highlights the essential roles played by GCNs in enhancing the classification accuracy of graphs. Furthermore, this new understanding enables us to overcome the limitations of existing pre-processing methods by proposing novel strategies, including designing a discriminative graph for GCN operation, recovering a missing and incomplete adjacency matrix from incomplete triple data, and achieving classified node detection in complete graphs. Experimental results show that addressing data issues through this new understanding significantly improves the performance, surpassing state-of-the-art baselines in certain cases.

We derive an effective field theory describing massive gravity through the conformal transformation of a Chern-Simons action, which also accounts for a scalar field. Upon analyzing this effective action, we identify two distinct types of solutions - spinning hairy black holes and stable solitons with scalar fields. Furthermore, by transforming both solutions to the Einstein frame, we demonstrate that they correspond to previously discovered black holes with masses and spins that can be adjusted. Ultimately, we establish the stability of the spinning soliton both thermodynamically and by perturbing its fields, confirming that the model produces a consistent representation of black holes with spins given by the square of their masses, mirroring a characteristic feature of quantum black holes.

Elastography, an advanced ultrasound imaging technique, provides a visual representation of tissue deformation in response to an applied stress. The diagnostic information derived from elastography is significantly enhanced by precisely positioning key features, measured in millimeters, identified in images constructed from ultrasonic data with slight shifts due to aberrations. This study introduces a precise and effective method, rooted in a novel approach called Virtual Origin Synthetic Aperture, for correcting lateral displacement errors. Inspired by Synthetic Aperture techniques, this method circumvents certain limitations of traditional compensatory methods, offering improved performance in positioning images constructed via Ray-tracing and Time-of-Flight Synthetic Aperture. A comparative analysis utilizing datasets from simulations and real ultrasound recordings demonstrates that this method consistently achieves sub-half-sample positioning accuracy, providing a precise reference framework for subsequent analyses in elastography.

Consider a scenario where a large language model is trained on procedural guides for various algorithms, then given the same inputs as a step-by-step demonstration of an algorithm's execution. Our examination of such a situation revealed three main components that effectively align the AI's predictions with actual output, for a wide range of puzzles. Initially, the AI's ability to follow along with a demonstration was compared to its capacity to merely follow steps, finding that synchronization with a demonstration significantly improves the alignment. Furthermore, we discovered two additional factors of connection, one involving internal structures similar to the demonstration and one of temporal organization, both of which contribute to the overall effect. Furthermore, two experiment types were performed to further understand this situation. Our findings from these experiments can be summarized as two main effects of connection, one reminiscent of components present in a demonstration and one of sequential organization, in an effort to better comprehend the overall effect. Our study successfully realigns the concept of following a demonstration in the context of modern neural systems.

Mean representation has become a fundamental concept in diverse fields including neuroscience, psychology, and marketing. Despite its utility, traditional methods fall short in capturing dimensionally rich data due to their reliance on static groupings, a problem exacerbated by the ever-increasing size and complexity of datasets. This research introduces a dynamic approach, the Adaptive Dynamic $k$-Means Grouping (ADKMG) model, capable of managing high-dimensionality data to identify and organize groups automatically. ADKMG integrates multiple, distinct information sources such as marketing, neuroscience, and psychological data. Employing the Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) method, our model efficiently processes large datasets and produces results that ensure statistical reliability while maintaining optimality. The ADKMG model exceeds the performance of current standard techniques in distinguishing and separating different information types, a problem mirrored in real-world applications.

A comprehensive analysis of SM predictions for $\mu^+ \gamma \rightarrow \mu^+ \gamma$ interactions was conducted, focusing on $t$-channel $W^{\pm}$ efficient estimations. Direct calculation shows that these $W^{\pm}$ contributions are negligible due to lepton universality, resulting in a suppression factor of approximately $10^{-3}$ compared to the contact interaction. When studying the magnitude of $W^{\pm}$ efficiency, various reference amplitudes were considered: the scalar amplitude experienced similar $s$- and $u$-channel suppression as the vector amplitude but with opposite interference patterns; meanwhile, the tensor amplitude exhibited the largest efficiency around 0.5 at 30 GeV photon energies. For lower energies below 30 GeV, the vector amplitude's interference leads to a higher $W^{\pm}$ efficiency, with an average value of $\langle e_{\rm eff}^2 \rangle \approx 0.16$ for $E_\gamma=10$ GeV and $\langle e_{\rm eff}^2 \rangle \approx 0.08$ for $E_\gamma=5$ GeV.

The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence, particularly in the field of deep neural networks, has resulted in models that excel at specific tasks but are often lacking in versatility. These highly specialized models are prone to catastrophic interference when learning new tasks, a problem caused by the non-modular nature of neural network representations. This research investigates the potential for organizing such networks into distinct functional modules using a novel modular learning algorithm, founded on the principle of mixture of experts. By imposing a structure that separates the networks into task-specific and shared modules, we aim to enhance their versatility in a model-free, multi-task reinforcement learning setting. Our approach demonstrates a significant advantage over conventional non-modular systems across four distinct scenarios in the multi-task version of the Mountain Car benchmark, achieving a 25% improvement in performance.

We present a formal system that replicates the statements proved undecidable in Godel's completeness theorem for first-order logic. This system demonstrates that, within a specific context of a decidable theory extending first-order logic, the decidability of a theory's axioms' consequences cannot be proven, thereby highlighting limitations similar to those found in Godel's first and second theorems, as well as in Tarski's undefinability of set theory's truth.

This research builds a 'spheres theorem' for functions in a specific category, referred to as spheres functions, which are defined within the framework of Clifford analysis. Specifically, functions are included in this category if they are square integrable on a three-dimensional space and satisfy a particular condition, denoted as (1.1). The study establishes an upper limit for the ratio between the square of the norm and the square of the average of these functions, using a constant of 2, or $2\frac{\|f\|^2}{\|\langle f\rangle\|^2}\leq$. Furthermore, it demonstrates that this ratio of 2, or more generally $\frac{\|f\|^2}{\|\langle f\rangle\|^2}=c$, results in functions that are combinations of three specific functions, each associated with a particular frequency, using the Helgerson-Lipschitz spheres functions as a basis. Notably, the techniques employed in this research are applicable to functions in a broader framework, referred to as monogenic functions, and establish that the ratio of 2, or more generally $\frac{\|f\|^2}{\|\langle f\rangle\|^2}=c$, results in functions that are weighted averages of three specific functions, each associated with a particular frequency, using the Helgerson-Lipschitz spheres functions as a basis.

In artificial intelligence, generating models that condition on specific inputs, particularly conditional generative adversarial networks (CGANs), has shown remarkable success. Despite this achievement, a critical aspect of probability generation remains unfulfilled for generative models, including CGANs. In certain applications, such as inverse challenges where a target image is generated and a process alters it, it is essential to be able to reconstruct the original from the modified version with a high level of accuracy. This requirement signifies that the generated probabilities must be consistent and that a model capable of learning this consistency, a forward-backward model, must be able to undo its work effectively. In the proposed approach, a simple regularization is applied to a CGAN to enable a forward-backward model to unlearn the simulated process, as long as the model consists of two standard components, namely a CGAN and two linear models representing the process. On real datasets and a collaborative challenge, the minimal regularization is found to improve performance substantially compared to a model without consistency, providing a standard for evaluating inconsistency in the field.

This research paper provides a proof that in certain fractional dynamical systems, there are no invariant curves in a unit space under specific contraction conditions. It also demonstrates that this issue is further complicated by offering examples of systems without invariant curves, yet they possess other characteristics, including periodic behavior and chaos, which are described with contrastive properties. Additionally, the study facilitates a fractional version of the Smith normal form, which is utilized in the analysis of linear components of these systems, along with its implications. Furthermore, the study presents methods for detecting chaos in these systems and their fractional equivalents, which are utilized to develop models and their linearizations, which are discussed in detail.

This research examines scintillation patterns in radio data from the pulsar PSR B1133+16 for a one-year period to characterize the interstellar environment around this highly active neutron star. By analyzing these patterns, researchers have been able to identify features within the surrounding space filled with gas. Some characteristics, such as small-scale density variations and interactions with galactic wind structures, are consistent with known properties of the local interstellar medium. Additionally, known properties of the pulsar and its surrounding environment have been used to better understand scintillation patterns. This knowledge has enabled estimates of key parameters, including those describing the surrounding space and the gas within the Milky Way's disk. Furthermore, known properties of the pulsar and its environment have been incorporated into a simulation to replicate scintillation patterns observed on the Earth. This in turn allows for comparisons between the actual measurements and the simulation results, thereby providing insights into the geometry and physical properties of the surrounding space and the gas within the Milky Way's disk.

A deep convolutional neural network framework called WaveNet has been proving highly effective in a variety of audio synthesis applications due to its superior performance. However, waveform generation at high sampling rates limits its practical use in real-time scenarios. This challenge can be addressed through real-time sampling techniques such as Multi-DilateNet. Our research builds upon WaveNet and Multi-DilatedNet by introducing a novel hybrid network that combines the strengths of both models, resulting in a cost-effective and efficient solution for high-fidelity audio generation. This new network leverages the sparse convolutional filtering of WaveNet, high sampling rate capability of Multi-DilatedNet, and unique features of pitch-sensitive network to create a cohesive and powerful generation system. We develop the PDCNet module, employing multiple stacking networks with varying dilation rates to achieve this goal. We integrate the PDCNet module into the existing WaveNet framework to form the proposed PDC-WaveNet model. Our extensive experiments using real-world datasets demonstrate the superiority of the PDC-WaveNet model in terms of both objective and subjective evaluation, outperforming the original WaveNet and other comparable autoregressive models and enabling practical applications of WaveNet at high sampling rates through the 100kHz condition.

The theory of shadows constitutes a novel bicategorical construct that extends the framework of truncations, adapting the intuitive concept of restricting to observable aspects of an category or bicategory. We establish a fundamental connection between the formation of shadows and the process of morphic insertion, demonstrating that insertion of morphisms can be characterized as the inverse of taking shadows. Consequently, truncation and morphic insertion form a coherent and interchangeable system, providing a reliable foundation for a local and global approach within the analysis of complex structures.

Our "Puzzle Sounds" project aims to realistically evaluate how effectively individuals can use sounds to navigate and pinpoint their position within both straightforward and intricate environments. We identify and categorize acoustic aspects that influence sound localization, using real architectural plans and simple models. A key feature of this work is the incorporation of complex structures often found in actual settings. We developed two distinct mockups spanning simple to intricate spatial configurations. A distinctive aspect of this study is the use of an auditory simulator for systematically exploring the environments and for conducting sound localization experiments with human subjects using Puzzle Sounds. A fully equipped anechoic chamber was utilized for these experiments, allowing us to present sounds to the participants via headphones in a realistic manner, emulating movement through the Puzzle Sounds scenarios. Initially used by volunteers for familiarization with the tasks, the Puzzle Sounds simulations were subsequently employed in an experimental setting for assessing their sound localization abilities. Over the course of the study, participants listened to sound simulations of navigating specific environments and were asked to pinpoint their location based on sounds produced by moving through Puzzle Sounds scenarios for various obstacles and ground surfaces. A comparative analysis was conducted to analyze the results, taking into consideration a random-guessing baseline. The evaluation demonstrated that even with complex spatial configurations, individuals can successfully identify their position within the environments based on sounds produced during their virtual traversal. Recent research indicates that using Euclidean distance in graph neural networks (GNNs) leads to degraded performance, particularly in scenarios involving the dynamic addition or removal of nodes. This research proposes replacing the commonly used convolution operation in sublinear GNNs with a Lorentzian distance convolution. This new approach leverages the hypothesis that many real-world graphs follow a scale-free distribution. By utilizing a Lorentzian convolution, parameters are automatically adjusted based on node features while maintaining the self-supervised learning advantage of GNNs. The resulting model, named LGCN (Lorentzian Graph Convolutional Network), demonstrates a 20% improvement in classification accuracy on static graphs and a 10% improvement in accuracy on changing graphs.

We present a new statistical model that extends the exponential distribution by incorporating the Tsallis distribution's features. This model, along with various generalizations, exhibits heavy-tailed or light-shaped distributions and can be applied to both economic and physical phenomena. We derive the maximum likelihood estimators for its parameters, compare their characteristics, and illustrate their use through estimation techniques and nonparametric density estimation. We also provide in-depth analyses using simulation studies and real-data applications, showing the model's versatility and potential advancements over related distributions. We demonstrate its calculation efficiency via an analytic expression for its cumulative distribution function, which allows the expected value of monotone functions to be calculated directly. We further generalize the model to include the Nakagami-L\'{e}vy, Pareto-L\'{e}vy, and Pareto distributions as special cases, and propose an exponential family representation for the original model and its Gamma generalization, along with a corresponding delayed version.

Similarities to a well-known "harmonic gauge" simplify the formulation of various higher-order gravity theories, such as $R^n$ heavy gravity, when a harmonic gauge is applied. This approach leads to a notable characteristic where the field's equation beyond a specific distance decreases significantly in $|g|\ll 1$ space. The adjustment to the theory with linear $R$ gravity results in a further decrease in order with $(\Box R)^2$ when the harmonic gauge is implemented. This effect also happens with f($R$) heavy gravity, but at a much higher distance due to the $|\Box| \ll 1$ reduction. The harmonic gauge directly reduces $| \Box \beta | \ll 1$ in a theory that includes General Relativity and $TR^2$ inflation, causing it to disappear completely in linear sigma models. These reductions often lead to the field's equation becoming algebraic in heavy gravity theories when $\Box$ is massive, as opposed to being distance-dependent when the harmonic gauge is not applied and $\Box$ is high-order. This distance-reducing approach also simplifies perturbation theory significantly, as seen with QUET gravity.

Recent research has converted the fundamental Poisson bracket equation, representing canonical conditions on a phase space, into a form compatible with Weyl-Wigner representation. This achievement is equivalent to the quantization process as first proposed by Jordan, Klein, and Wu. We illustrate this equivalence by transforming the non-relativistic Schrödinger equation from its initial brute-force approach to its Weyl-Wigner form, before deriving the non-relativistic Schrödinger equation from its canonical conditions.

The notion of negative absolute temperature, which has been disputed for many years, is re-examined in this investigation. It is re-interpreted in a way that demonstrates its validity, without considering spontaneous processes. Based on the Schrodinger distribution and canonical ensemble, we show that temperatures below zero are associated with highly energetic states, which do not occur in everyday situations but are plausible given certain conditions. We derive a formula calculating the average energy of the Schrodinger distribution to illustrate this point.

Researchers have examined the implications of the most basic scoto-seesaw model, incorporating the smallest possible dark sector consisting of a singlet scalar and an inert dark matter fermion. By analyzing the full range of parameters, they investigated several key aspects including the consistency of the dark sector, mechanisms for neutrino generation via the scoto-seesaw framework, and signals of new physics at particle colliders. They discovered that the easiest variant of this model can account for neutrino phenomena with a specific parameter configuration, leading to a prediction for the dark matter fermion's mass within a particular range of a coupling constant that also produces testable deviations from the Standard Model at the Large Hadron Collider in the tens of GeV domain. However, this easiest version of the model fails to stabilize the electroweak vacuum.

Investigating the absorption spectra of isolated Cu+ and low-spin Fe2+ ions using a theoretical approach, we employed multi-configuration time-dependent Hartree--Fock and stochastic time-dependent Hartree--Fock methods to calculate dipole transitions from the ground electronic state to excited states with multiplicities of quintuplet, triplet, and doublet, as well as sextuplet, quartuplet, triplet, doublet, and doublet states. The results indicate that $t_{2g}$ to $e_g$ orbital transitions possess higher intensities than previously believed, possessing approximately a 10% contribution to the total absorption. Consequently, in compounds containing 4d and 5d transition metals with $t_{2g}$ to $e_g$ symmetry, electron reorganization rates may be significantly overestimated if experimental data is fitted with continuous time-dependent population components with the same symmetry.

Rational blow-downs are a type of surgical procedure on smooth 4-dimensional manifolds that can alter the quantum homology of a manifold. In this study, we investigate the impact of these procedures on the quantum homology of a specific class of manifolds, focusing on the Birkhoff ball blow-up. We find that this operation modifies the quantum homology by a factor of a specific polynomial to a shifted and twisted version of the quantum homology of the original manifold. As a consequence of this result, we are able to distinguish the Birkhoff ball blow-up from other types of ball blow-ups with smaller knot components, by examining the quantum homology of the underlying manifold.

Multidimensional data visualization is essential for effective information discovery and decision-making in various fields, yet existing linear visualization tools limit the examination of data relationships by failing to support nonlinear transformations. This is particularly restrictive when a non-linear data format is necessary for optimal pattern recognition and knowledge acquisition. ViDaExpert, a novel interactive visualization instrument, overcomes these obstacles by integrating a wide range of nonlinear transformation methods, including neural networks, tree-based models, tree-based permutation importance, general additive models, and various noise and transformation techniques. With user-friendly features for visualization, this instrument enables robust explanation and understanding of data. ViDaExpert is built in R using the Shiny framework and comes with preinstalled packages for common statistical and machine learning methods, as well as ROCR for performance assessment visualization. This instrument is demonstrated through multiple cases involving real-world datasets.
